title: Clinicians push back on medical AI beyond diagnostics, citing thin performance data
subtitle: A Financial Times survey published September 20 finds physicians and nurses are willing to trust AI for imaging and triage, but wary of its use in prescribing, dosing, and treatment planning — where the outcomes data does not yet exist.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Financial Times reported on Sunday, September 20, that clinicians are drawing a sharper line between diagnostic AI — which they largely accept — and AI applied to prescribing, dosing, and treatment planning, which they are pushing back on for lack of clinical outcome data. The reporting builds on the 2026 Wolters Kluwer Future Ready Healthcare survey, run with Ipsos among 355 US physicians and nurses in March, which named advertiser-driven bias (72%), deskilling (74%), and hallucinations (74%) as top-tier concerns, and found that only 27% of respondents were aware of a formal AI governance policy at their institution — up from 21% in 2025.

The gap between adoption and governance is the interesting part. Doximity's 2026 State of AI in Medicine report has physician daily AI use at 63% in January 2026, up from 47% a year earlier, with family medicine at 88% daily usage and neurology leading adoption at 64%. Literature search and voice-based documentation are the top workflows. What clinicians are not adopting at the same rate is AI in the treatment-planning loop, and the FT's reporting suggests why: the clinical trials that would tell them whether an AI-suggested dose adjustment improves patient outcomes have mostly not been run yet, and the FDA's clearance pathway for AI medical devices — 1,357 cleared as of the August PLOS study — has been criticized for accepting bench-test evidence in place of prospective patient-outcome data.

This pattern is worth watching because it is going to determine where the second half of the medical AI market is built. The imaging-and-scribe layer is close to saturated: RadNet, Aidoc, Nuance DAX, Abridge, and Suki have most of the enterprise beachheads. The next wave — treatment recommendation, clinical decision support, autonomous dosing — is where the revenue is, and where the clinician trust does not yet exist. Insilico's Phase III start for the fully AI-designed drug rentosertib in July, and Corvista's July FDA clearance for AI PCWP heart-failure detection, are both signals that the trials are coming. The story on Sunday is that the trials have not arrived yet, and clinicians know it.

Takeaway for learners — if you are studying medical AI, or working in one, this is the honest version of the field's status: the imaging and documentation layer has cleared the trust bar, the treatment layer has not, and closing the gap requires prospective outcome trials that most current products have not run. If you evaluate a medical AI product, ask three questions: What patient outcome does it change, in what population, with what effect size, on what evidence. If a vendor cannot answer those in a sentence each, they are selling you a scribe or an imaging tool with a bigger label, not a treatment tool. That distinction is doing all the work in what clinicians will and will not adopt.
